questions.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $G$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $G,$ then $G$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $G=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $G,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
G={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}G & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -5 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-16 & 9 \\ -30 & 17\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
M={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[8]{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[4]{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $M=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${M}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{M}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

$$

$$

questions.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $T$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]T=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $T:$

$$
T={{{[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $T$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $T$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ 3 & -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -7\end{aligned}]$

N={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $N$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $N$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find a $2 \times 2$ matrix $C$ that has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=1$ and $\lambda_2=-4,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $\mathcal{B}= \{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $C,$ then $C$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $C=PDP^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $C,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order: 

$$
[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]
$$

Let $[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -2 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2} & -\frac{5}{2} \\ -\frac{5}{2} & -\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Raising a Matrix to a Large Power Using the Properties of Diagonalization
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First,  notice that

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Since $A=PDP^{-1},$ we can compute $A^k$ by using the formula 

$$
A^{k} = PD^{k}P^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{100} & =P{D}^{100}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{100}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{100} & 0 \\ 0 & {0}^{100}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors of a Matrix Using the Properties of Diagonalization
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2 \times 2$ matrix $E,$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $E\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, $E$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $E$ are $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=6$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-3}[\begin{aligned}1 & -6 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} & 2 \\ \frac{1}{3} & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$
